claim: Sensory feedback is widely accepted as an integral component of vertebrate locomotor control.
source: Sensory feedback is widely accepted as an integral component of vertebrate locomotor control (Cohen, 1992; Donelan and Pearson, 2004; Grillner, 2011; Prochazka and Ellaway, 2012; Rossignol et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Proprioception from muscle mechanoreceptors contributes to short-latency reflexes via spinal mono- and polysynaptic pathways to regulate ongoing muscle activity and mechanical output.
source: Proprioception from muscle mechanoreceptors contributes to 1) short-latency reflexes via spinal mono- and polysynaptic pathways to regulate the ongoing activity and muscle mechanical output (force, stiffness, impedance and work)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established research in the field.

claim: Proprioception from muscle mechanoreceptors contributes to longer-latency responses to coordinate and maintain task-level goals for balance and movement.
source: Proprioception from muscle mechanoreceptors contributes to 1) short-latency reflexes via spinal mono- and polysynaptic pathways to regulate the ongoing activity and muscle mechanical output (force, stiffness, impedance and work) and 2) longer-latency responses to coordinate and maintain task-level goals for balance and movement (Grillner, 2011; Lam and Pearson, 2002; Frigon and Rossignol, 2006; Prochazka and Ellaway, 2012; Proske and Gandevia, 2012; Rossignol et al., 2006; Safavynia and Ting, 2013; Sherrington and Laslett, 1903; Sherrington, 1910).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Proprioceptive reflexes can occur through autogenic pathways arising from the same muscle.
source: Proprioceptive reflexes can occur through autogenic (self-generated) pathways arising from the same muscle, and through heterogenic pathways arising from other muscles via spinal interneurons (Abelew et al., 2000; Frigon and Rossignol, 2006; Lam and Pearson, 2002; Nichols, 1989; Ross and Nichols, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Proprioceptive reflexes can occur through heterogenic pathways arising from other muscles via spinal interneurons.
source: Proprioceptive reflexes can occur through autogenic (self-generated) pathways arising from the same muscle, and through heterogenic pathways arising from other muscles via spinal interneurons (Abelew et al., 2000; Frigon and Rossignol, 2006; Lam and Pearson, 2002; Nichols, 1989; Ross and Nichols, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Sensorimotor delay constrains how quickly an animal can sense and respond to a stimulus using feedback control.
source: Sensorimotor delay constrains how quickly an animal can sense and respond to a stimulus using feedback control (More and Donelan, 2018; More et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The fastest possible feedback loop occurs through mono-synaptic reflexes, which involve a delay that increases in proportion to nerve transmission distance.
source: The fastest possible feedback loop occurs through mono-synaptic reflexes, which involve a delay that increases in proportion to nerve transmission distance.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of neural physiology.

claim: Reflex delay becomes a larger fraction of the stride cycle with increasing speed, limiting time available for reflex-mediated correction.
source: This reflex delay becomes a larger fraction of the stride cycle with increasing speed, limiting time available for reflex-mediated correction.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the relationship between fixed delays and variable stride cycle times.

claim: Long delays relative to stride cycle times likely necessitate greater reliance on feedforward control strategies at higher speeds.
source: The challenges of long delays relative to stride cycle times likely necessitates greater reliance on feedforward control strategies at higher speeds.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the constraints of sensorimotor delays.

claim: Rhythmic spinal networks can generate the basic flexion and extension motor pattern for gait, even when proprioceptive feedback is removed.
source: Rhythmic spinal networks can generate the basic flexion and extension motor pattern for gait, even when proprioceptive feedback is removed (e.g., Pearson et al., 2003; Sharp and Bekoff, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Feedforward motor activation coupled to intrinsic muscle properties can be sufficient to produce stable gait.
source: Although feedforward networks normally act in concert with feedback, feedforward motor activation coupled to intrinsic muscle properties can be sufficient to produce stable gait (Yakovenko et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The lateral gastrocnemius of guinea fowl rapidly absorbs energy in response to unexpected drop perturbations, stabilizing high speed running without a reflex response.
source: Consistent with this, the lateral gastrocnemius (LG) of guinea fowl (Numida meleagris) rapidly absorbs energy in response to unexpected drop perturbations (Daley et al., 2009), stabilizing high speed running without a reflex response.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The rapid perturbation response in guinea fowl LG arises from the intrinsic mechanical properties of the muscle-tendon tissues and musculoskeletal system.
source: The rapid perturbation response arises from the intrinsic mechanical properties of the muscle-tendon tissues and musculoskeletal system (Brown and Loeb, 2000; Loeb et al., 1999; Jindrich and Full, 2002; Azizi et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Intrinsic mechanical responses can be actively tuned by the specific feedforward pattern of muscle activation.
source: Intrinsic mechanical responses can be actively tuned by the specific feedforward pattern of muscle activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by examples from the literature cited in the following sentences.

claim: Humans hopping on surfaces with randomized, sudden increases in ground stiffness show a feedforward increase in muscle co-activation and knee flexion, increasing mechanical stability.
source: For example, humans hopping on surfaces with randomized, sudden increases in ground stiffness show a feedforward increase in muscle co-activation and knee flexion, increasing mechanical stability (Moritz and Farley, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Guinea fowl running over obstacles use a combination of feedforward, intrinsic mechanical and reflex-mediated mechanisms, with a delay of ~40 ms for reflex-mediated increases in muscle force.
source: Guinea fowl running over obstacles use a combination of feedforward, intrinsic mechanical and reflex-mediated mechanisms, with a delay of ~40 ms for reflex-mediated increases in muscle force (6ms reflex latency + 34ms force development delay: Daley et al., 2009; Daley and Biewener, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Self-reinnervation involves peripheral nerve branch transection and immediate repair, resulting in recovery of motor output with long-term, local loss of autogenic muscle proprioception.
source: Self-reinnervation involves peripheral nerve branch transection and immediate repair, resulting in recovery of motor output with long-term, local loss of autogenic muscle proprioception (Cope et al., 1994; Bullinger et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Self-reinnervation occurs through axonal regrowth and reconnection with denervated tissues over a recovery period of 4-8 weeks.
source: Self-reinnervation occurs through axonal regrowth and reconnection with denervated tissues over a recovery period of 4-8 weeks (Carr et al., 2010; Cope et al., 1994; Gordon and Stein, 1982; Vannucci et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Reinnervated muscles retain a deficit in the monosynaptic stretch reflex due to synaptic retraction of primary muscle spindle afferents and disconnection from parent motoneuron populations.
source: Reinnervated muscles retain a deficit in the monosynaptic stretch reflex due to synaptic retraction of primary muscle spindle afferents and disconnection from parent motoneuron populations (Alvarez et al., 2011; Brandt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Intermuscular force and length feedback networks may remain partially intact in reinnervated muscles.
source: However, intermuscular force and length feedback networks may remain partially intact (Lyle et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Cats and rats with reinnervated muscles maintain whole-limb function by adjusting inter-joint coordination and muscle co-activation to compensate for lost reflex-mediated ankle stiffness.
source: Cats and rats with reinnervated muscles maintain whole-limb function by adjusting inter-joint coordination and muscle co-activation to compensate for loss of reflex-mediated ankle stiffness (Abelew et al., 2000; Maas et al., 2007; Chang et al., 2009; Boeltz et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Birds share features of sensorimotor structure and function with mammals, including muscle tissue properties.
source: Birds share features of sensorimotor structure and function with mammals, including muscle tissue properties (Nelson et al., 2004; Poore et al., 1997) and muscle proprioception through muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organs (Dorward, 1970; Haiden and Awad, 1981; Maier, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Birds have muscle proprioception through muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organs.
source: Birds share features of sensorimotor structure and function with mammals, including muscle tissue properties (Nelson et al., 2004; Poore et al., 1997) and muscle proprioception through muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organs (Dorward, 1970; Haiden and Awad, 1981; Maier, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Ground birds use bipedal walking and running gaits with mechanics and energetics similar to human locomotion.
source: Ground birds use bipedal walking and running gaits with mechanics and energetics similar to human locomotion (Heglund et al., 1982; Taylor et al., 1982; Gatesy and Biewener, 1991; Roberts et al., 1997; Daley and Birn-Jeffery, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Reinnervated and intact LG exhibit similar steady state mechanical function.
source: We find that many features of the steady-state in vivo mechanical function of the guinea fowl reinnervated lateral gastrocnemius (rLG) are similar to that previously measured in the intact LG (iLG) (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Reinnervated and intact LG exhibit similar work modulation in response to obstacle encounters.
source: Reinnervated and intact LG exhibit similar steady state mechanical function and similar work modulation in response to obstacle encounters.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reinnervated LG exhibits 23ms earlier steady-state activation compared to intact LG.
source: Reinnervated LG exhibits 23ms earlier steady-state activation, consistent with feedforward tuning of activation phase to compensate for lost proprioception.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Earlier steady-state activation in reinnervated LG is consistent with feedforward tuning of activation phase to compensate for lost proprioception.
source: Reinnervated LG exhibits 23ms earlier steady-state activation, consistent with feedforward tuning of activation phase to compensate for lost proprioception.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data based on inference about compensatory mechanisms.

claim: Modulation of activity duration is impaired in reinnervated LG.
source: Modulation of activity duration is impaired in rLG, confirming the role of reflex feedback in regulating force duration in intact muscle.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Impaired modulation of activity duration in reinnervated LG confirms the role of reflex feedback in regulating force duration in intact muscle.
source: Modulation of activity duration is impaired in rLG, confirming the role of reflex feedback in regulating force duration in intact muscle.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data based on inference about the role of reflexes.

claim: During the swing phase of the stride cycle, both intact and reinnervated LG exhibit a period of passive stretch, followed by rapid shortening.
source: During the swing phase of the stride cycle, both iLG and rLG exhibit a period of passive stretch, followed by rapid shortening.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Activation and force development in LG begin in late swing around the time of the transition from stretch to shortening.
source: Activation and force development begin in late swing around the time of the transition from stretch to shortening, initiating rapid active shortening until foot contact (Figure 2, triangles).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: At the time of foot contact, LG force increases rapidly to a peak before midstance, then declines more slowly.
source: At the time of foot contact, force increases rapidly to a peak before midstance, then declines more slowly.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In level running both intact and reinnervated LG show a near-isometric phase in early stance, followed by shortening in late stance, which produces net positive work.
source: Typically, in level running both iLG and rLG show a near-isometric phase in early stance, followed by shortening in late stance, which produces net positive work, as indicated by counter-clockwise force-length work loops (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The average magnitude of work output during steady level running is similar between intact and reinnervated LG.
source: The average magnitude of work output (Wnet) during steady level running is similar between the iLG and rLG, with similar spread of the distribution around the mean (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Reinnervated LG shows faster shortening velocity at peak force compared to intact LG across both level and obstacle terrains.
source: However, rLG shows faster shortening velocity at peak force (VpkF) compared to the iLG across both level and obstacle terrains (Figure 4), indicating a difference in steady state contraction dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Faster shortening velocity at peak force in reinnervated LG indicates a difference in steady state contraction dynamics.
source: However, rLG shows faster shortening velocity at peak force (VpkF) compared to the iLG across both level and obstacle terrains (Figure 4), indicating a difference in steady state contraction dynamics.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data based on inference.

claim: During obstacle encounters, foot contact with the obstacle occurs earlier in the stride cycle compared to level terrain, altering force-length dynamics during the obstacle stance period.
source: In obstacle encounters (Figure 2, S 0), foot contact with the obstacle occurs earlier in the stride cycle compared to level terrain, altering force-length dynamics during the obstacle stance period.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: During obstacle contact, both intact and reinnervated LG remain at longer lengths, force increases rapidly to reach a higher peak force, and the muscle shortens throughout force development, producing positive work.
source: During obstacle contact, both iLG and rLG remain at longer lengths, force increases rapidly to reach a higher peak force, and the muscle shortens throughout force development, producing positive work (Figure 2, S 0).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Both intact and reinnervated LG exhibit increased force and work output in obstacle strides compared to level strides.
source: Both iLG and rLG exhibit increased force and work output in obstacle strides compared to level strides (Figure 3, S 0).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The magnitude of the shift in work output in obstacle strides is similar between intact and reinnervated cohorts, increasing by 3.60±0.57 Jkg−1 in intact LG and 3.88±0.60 Jkg−1 in reinnervated LG.
source: The magnitude of the shift in work output (Wnet) in obstacle strides (S 0) is similar between intact and reinnervated cohorts, increasing by 3.60±0.57 Jkg−1 in iLG and 3.88±0.60 Jkg−1 in rLG (mean±95% ci, Figure 4B, Table 2 ).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Table 2.

claim: In intact LG, increased work upon obstacle contact occurs through modest increases in both peak force and shortening velocity, compared to level strides.
source: In iLG, increased work upon obstacle contact occurs through modest increases in both peak force (Fpk) and shortening velocity (VpkF), compared to level strides.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Table 2.

claim: Reinnervated LG exhibits a substantially larger increase in peak force on obstacle strides and maintains similar shortening velocity between level and obstacle terrain strides.
source: In contrast, rLG exhibits a substantially larger increase in Fpk on obstacle strides and maintains similar VpkF between level and obstacle terrain strides (S 0, Figure 4B, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Table 2.

claim: Reinnervated LG exhibits small but significant increases in peak force in the strides preceding and following obstacle contact compared to level terrain.
source: Reinnervated LG also exhibits small but significant increases in Fpk in the strides preceding and following obstacle contact (S-1 and S+1, respectively), compared to level terrain.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Table 2.

claim: Reinnervated LG and intact LG show similar increases in total muscle activation intensity in obstacle strides compared to steady level strides.
source: Despite deficits in LG monosynaptic reflex following reinnervation, rLG and iLG show similar increases in total muscle activation intensity (Etot, integral of EMG) in obstacle strides compared to steady level strides (S 0, Figure 5).

claim: Intact LG exhibits a 4% increase in duration in obstacle strides compared to level.
source: Intact LG exhibits a 4% increase in duration in obstacle strides (S 0) compared to level; however, there is no significant increase in EMG duration for rLG in S 0 (Figure 5B, Table 2).

claim: There is no significant increase in EMG duration for reinnervated LG in obstacle strides.
source: Intact LG exhibits a 4% increase in duration in obstacle strides (S 0) compared to level; however, there is no significant increase in EMG duration for rLG in S 0 (Figure 5B, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Table 2.

claim: The observed increase in total EMG activity in reinnervated LG obstacle strides occurs through increased activation amplitude, not increased duration.
source: This suggest that the observed increase in Etot in rLG obstacle strides occurs through increased activation amplitude, not increased duration.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data showing increased total EMG without increased duration.

claim: Reinnervated LG exhibits longer steady-state duration of activity compared to intact LG across all level and obstacle terrain strides, averaging 37% of the stride cycle in reinnervated LG compared to 29% in intact LG.
source: Reinnervated LG exhibits longer steady-state duration of activity (Edur) compared to iLG across all level and obstacle terrain strides, averaging 37% of the stride cycle in rLG compared to 29% in iLG (Figure 5B, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Table 2.

claim: Reinnervated LG exhibits higher average frequency of EMG activity across all strides compared to the intact cohort.
source: Additionally, rLG exhibits higher average frequency of EMG activity across all strides compared to the intact cohort (Figure 5, Table 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5, Table 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The steady-state timing of reinnervated LG activation is phase-shifted to 6% (23ms) earlier in the stride cycle relative to the length trajectory.
source: Finally, the steady-state timing of rLG activation is phase-shifted to 6% (23ms) earlier in the stride cycle relative to the length trajectory, quantified by the variable 'Ephase' (Figure 6, Tables 1–2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Tables 1-2.

claim: Earlier activation onset may help explain the higher rate of shortening in reinnervated LG compared to intact LG.
source: Earlier activation onset may help explain the higher rate of shortening in rLG compared to iLG, reported above.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the observed data.

claim: Increased EMG activity begins ~30-40 ms before obstacle-induced increases in length and force, for both intact and reinnervated LG, suggesting an anticipatory (feedforward) contribution to increases in total EMG activity.
source: Increased EMG activity begins ~30-40 ms before obstacle-induced increases in length and force, for both iLG and rLG, suggesting an anticipatory (feedforward) contribution to increases in Etot (Figure 7, arrows indicating 'anticipatory increase').
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7 and inference about the timing of the response.

claim: In intact LG, the anticipatory increase in EMG starts ~25% of stride period.
source: In iLG, the anticipatory increase in EMG starts ~25% of stride period (asterisk in EMG trace and vertical dashed line in Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In intact LG, starting around 58% of stride period, there is another distinct burst of increased activity, suggesting reflex-mediated contribution to increased EMG in obstacle strides.
source: Starting around 58% of stride period, there is another distinct burst of increased activity, suggesting reflex-mediated contribution to increased EMG in obstacle strides (Figure 7, arrow indicating 'reflex').
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7 and inference about the mechanism.

claim: In reinnervated LG, the 'anticipatory increase' in EMG starts around 21% of stride.
source: In rLG, the 'anticipatory increase' in EMG starts around 21% of stride (asterisk and vertical dashed line in 7B)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Activity in the latter half of stance in reinnervated LG is highly variable and idiosyncratic among individuals.
source: however activity in the latter half of stance is highly variable and idiosyncratic among individuals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), as indicated by the wide 95% confidence intervals spanning the region of time where the iLG shows a distinct reflex response (compare Figure 7B versus 7A lower panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cross-correlation between the obstacle perturbation trajectories for intact LG reveals a correlation of 0.82 between length and EMG deviations, and a correlation of 0.85 between force and EMG deviations.
source: Cross-correlation between the obstacle perturbation trajectories for iLG reveals a correlation of 0.82 between length and EMG deviations, and a correlation of 0.85 between force and EMG deviations.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the text.

claim: For reinnervated LG, the cross-correlations are reduced to 0.53 between length and EMG deviations, and 0.57 between force and EMG deviations.
source: For rLG, the cross-correlations are reduced to 0.53 between length and EMG deviations, and 0.57 between force and EMG deviations, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the text.

claim: The reduced correlations suggest a disrupted reflex-mediated response to muscle load and strain in the latter half of stance in reinnervated LG, but which is present in intact LG.
source: The reduced correlations suggest a disrupted reflex-mediated response to muscle load and strain in the latter half of stance in rLG, but which is present in iLG (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the correlation data.

claim: Birds with reinnervated LG exhibit more pronounced shifts in gait dynamics in obstacle terrain relative to level terrain compared to the intact cohort.
source: Compared to the intact cohort, birds with rLG exhibit more pronounced shifts in gait dynamics in obstacle terrain relative to level terrain.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Obstacle-induced increases in peak force are larger for reinnervated LG compared to intact LG.
source: Obstacle-induced increases in peak force (Fpk) are larger for rLG compared to iLG (S 0 Figure 4, Table 2), reflecting larger deviations from steady state in response to the same obstacle.

claim: Larger obstacle-induced increases in peak force in reinnervated LG reflect larger deviations from steady state in response to the same obstacle.
source: Obstacle-induced increases in peak force (Fpk) are larger for rLG compared to iLG (S 0 Figure 4, Table 2), reflecting larger deviations from steady state in response to the same obstacle.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data.

claim: Reinnervated LG shows small but significant increases in peak force in the strides preceding and following obstacle contact compared to steady level strides.
source: Additionally, rLG shows small but significant increases in peak force (Fpk) in the strides preceding and following obstacle contact (S -1, S +1) compared to steady level strides (Figure 4B, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Table 2.

claim: Multiple significant differences from level strides occur for reinnervated LG in the stride following obstacle contact, including a 39±22% increase in total EMG activity, a 6±2% decrease in force duration and a 4±3% decrease in stride duration.
source: Multiple significant differences from level strides occur for rLG in S +1, including a 39±22% increase in Etot, a 6±2% decrease in force duration and a 4±3% decrease in stride duration (mean±95% ci, Table 2).

claim: Most variables for intact LG have recovered to steady state in the stride following obstacle contact.
source: In contrast, most variables for iLG have recovered to steady state in S +1 (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Table 2.

claim: Reinnervated LG shows larger deviations from steady state, and a slower recovery to steady state mechanics and activation level compared to intact LG, indicating reduced stability.
source: However, rLG shows larger deviations from steady state, and a slower recovery to steady state mechanics and activation level compared to iLG, indicating reduced stability.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data based on inference about stability.

claim: Reinnervated birds show differences in running kinematics in obstacle terrain compared to the intact cohort, undergoing a more pronounced increase in ankle flexion in obstacle encounters.
source: Reinnervated birds also show differences in running kinematics in obstacle terrain compared to the intact cohort, undergoing a more pronounced increase in ankle flexion in obstacle encounters (Figure 8).

claim: Reinnervated birds use a shorter stride duration immediately preceding the obstacle encounter, suggesting anticipatory preparation that is not observed in intact birds.
source: Reinnervated birds also use a shorter stride duration immediately preceding the obstacle encounter (S -1), suggesting anticipatory preparation that is not observed in intact birds (Figure 8).

source: These observations suggest reduced ankle stiffness and increased anticipatory preparation for obstacle encounters in the reinnervated birds.

claim: Birds with intact LG proprioception use feedforward and feedback regulation of muscle activity to maintain stability in obstacle terrain.
source: In concert with the stabilizing contributions of the intrinsic muscle-tendon dynamics, guinea fowl with intact proprioception also use feedforward and feedback regulation of muscle activity to maintain stability in obstacle terrain, with greater feedforward contributions when obstacles are visible and high contrast (Daley and Biewener, 2011; Gordon et al., 2015).

claim: Guinea fowl with intact proprioception show greater feedforward contributions to muscle activity when obstacles are visible and high contrast.
source: In concert with the stabilizing contributions of the intrinsic muscle-tendon dynamics, guinea fowl with intact proprioception also use feedforward and feedback regulation of muscle activity to maintain stability in obstacle terrain, with greater feedforward contributions when obstacles are visible and high contrast (Daley and Biewener, 2011; Gordon et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Guinea fowl with LG proprioceptive deficit achieve similar increases in total EMG activity during obstacle strides; however, the increases in activity occur early in the stride, before obstacle-induced changes in muscle force and length.
source: We find that guinea fowl with LG proprioceptive deficit achieve similar increases in total EMG activity during obstacle strides; however, the increases in activity occur early in the stride, before obstacle-induced changes in muscle force and length (Figure 7).

claim: The early increases in EMG activity in reinnervated LG are consistent with anticipatory, feedforward increases in neural drive to the muscle.
source: This is consistent with anticipatory, feedforward increases in neural drive to the muscle, as observed in birds running over high-contrast visible obstacles (Gordon et al., 2015), and humans hopping on randomized but expected increases in surface stiffness (Moritz and Farley, 2004).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data and comparison to cited research.

claim: The reinnervated LG contributes to an effective obstacle negotiation response, but requires a longer recovery time and increased muscle activity following obstacle contact.

claim: Similar increases in work output in response to obstacle encounters in reinnervated and intact LG is consistent with the idea that muscle work modulation is an important feature of task-level control for stability in uneven terrain.

This finding is consistent with the idea that muscle work modulation is an important feature of task-level control for stability in uneven terrain (Daley et al., 2009; Daley and Biewener, 2011).

claim: Work modulation is achieved through different underlying mechanisms in reinnervated and intact LG.
source: However, work modulation is achieved through different underlying mechanisms in rLG and iLG.

claim: Earlier steady state activation in reinnervated LG enables higher muscle force development in early stance to resist the external load applied at foot contact.
source: Earlier steady state activation in rLG (lacking autogenic proprioceptive feedback) enables higher muscle force development in early stance to resist the external load applied at foot contact, which likely contributes to the higher rate of shortening throughout stance.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data and understanding of muscle mechanics.

claim: Earlier steady state activation in reinnervated LG likely contributes to the higher rate of shortening throughout stance.
source: Earlier steady state activation in rLG (lacking autogenic proprioceptive feedback) enables higher muscle force development in early stance to resist the external load applied at foot contact, which likely contributes to the higher rate of shortening throughout stance.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data and understanding of muscle mechanics.

claim: The increase in peak force in reinnervated LG obstacle encounters includes an active contribution from increased feedforward drive and EMG amplitude.
source: This increase in peak force likely involves both active and passive components: an active contribution from increased feedforward drive and EMG amplitude (Figure 5B), and a passive contribution from increased stretch of connective tissues associated with a more flexed ankle posture at foot contact (Figure 8).

claim: The increase in peak force in reinnervated LG obstacle encounters includes a passive contribution from increased stretch of connective tissues associated with a more flexed ankle posture at foot contact.
source: This increase in peak force likely involves both active and passive components: an active contribution from increased feedforward drive and EMG amplitude (Figure 5B), and a passive contribution from increased stretch of connective tissues associated with a more flexed ankle posture at foot contact (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Birds with reinnervated LG show an anticipatory shift in stride duration before obstacle encounters, which is not observed in the intact cohort.
source: Finally, Birds with rLG also show an anticipatory shift in stride duration before obstacle encounters, which is not observed in the intact cohort (Figure 8B) and may help control landing conditions for obstacle encounters (Gordon et al., 2015).

claim: The anticipatory shift in stride duration before obstacle encounters in reinnervated birds may help control landing conditions for obstacle encounters.
source: Finally, Birds with rLG also show an anticipatory shift in stride duration before obstacle encounters, which is not observed in the intact cohort (Figure 8B) and may help control landing conditions for obstacle encounters (Gordon et al., 2015).
